title: WERE THE NEPHILIM REALLY GIANTS?
paragraphs: The Ancient Mystery That Refuses to Die
For centuries, readers have stumbled upon a strange group mentioned only briefly in Scripture and then vanished into mystery almost as quickly as they appeared.
A name that has inspired countless documentaries, conspiracy theories, fantasy novels, YouTube rabbit holes, and debates among Christians, skeptics, historians, and scholars alike.
Or is there something much deeper happening in the text than most people realize?
What if the greatest mystery of the Nephilim is not their size...
but what they reveal about the human heart?
Because beneath all the fascination with giants lies a far more terrifying reality.
And a world that looked disturbingly similar to our own.
Vayyir'u bene ha'elohim et benot ha'adam.
"The sons of God saw that the daughters of man were beautiful."
The phrase "sons of God" in Hebrew is:
This phrase appears elsewhere in the Old Testament.
In Job 1:6, Job 2:1, and Job 38:7, it refers to heavenly beings who present themselves before God.
This has led many scholars throughout history to conclude that Genesis 6 is describing supernatural beings interacting with humanity.
"The Nephilim were on the earth in those days..."
The word Nephilim comes from the Hebrew root:
This is why many translators and scholars connect Nephilim with the idea of "fallen ones."
However, Scripture itself never explicitly defines the word.
And that is where the debate begins.
Surprisingly, the Hebrew word Nephilim does not directly mean "giants."
The idea largely comes from the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament known as the Septuagint.
This Greek term became the source of the English concept of giants.
But in ancient Greek literature, gigantes did not necessarily mean enormous people.
It often referred to mighty warriors, powerful beings, or figures associated with rebellion against divine authority.
In other words, the Greek word carries more meaning than simply height.
The image of massive humans likely developed over time through interpretation and later traditions.
Yet there is a reason many believers still associate the Nephilim with extraordinary size.
Numbers 13:32-33 records the spies entering Canaan.
"There we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers."
The descendants of Anak were known for unusual stature.
This passage clearly presents them as physically intimidating.
However, careful readers should notice something important.
The report comes from fearful spies.
These same spies exaggerated multiple details because of their fear and unbelief.
God later rebukes them for spreading a bad report.
So while the Anakim were certainly formidable people, some scholars caution against taking every detail of their description literally.
Fear often makes enemies look bigger than they really are.
Human history has not changed much.
For nearly two thousand years, Christians have generally held one of three primary interpretations.
This interpretation argues that the "sons of God" were angelic beings.
This was the dominant understanding among many ancient Jewish writings before Christ.
The Book of Enoch, though not Scripture, reflects this perspective.
Supporters point to Job's use of Bene Ha'Elohim and to New Testament passages such as Jude 6-7 and 2 Peter 2:4-5, where angels are connected with extraordinary rebellion before the Flood.
This view became popular among many church fathers.
It argues that the "sons of God" were the godly descendants of Seth, while the "daughters of men" were descendants of Cain.
The focus is not angelic corruption but spiritual compromise through ungodly intermarriage.
Supporters emphasize that Jesus taught angels do not marry.
A third interpretation suggests powerful kings or rulers called themselves divine sons and abused their authority by taking women as they pleased.
Ancient Near Eastern rulers often claimed special divine status.
This view highlights oppression, power, and human corruption.
Faithful Bible-believing scholars can be found on all sides of the discussion.
This is where many discussions go wrong.
People become obsessed with mysteries God only briefly mentions.
Meanwhile they overlook what God spends an entire chapter emphasizing.
Genesis 6 is not primarily about Nephilim.
The chapter's emotional center arrives in Genesis 6:5.
"The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth."
The Hebrew word for wickedness is:
Then comes one of the most heartbreaking verses in the Bible.
"The LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and it grieved Him to His heart."
"He was deeply pained in His heart."
The focus is not giant anatomy.
The focus is a grieving God watching His creation destroy itself.
Many people read Genesis 6 looking for monsters.
They miss the monster staring back from the mirror.
The chapter reveals humanity's ability to corrupt everything God creates.
The earth becomes filled with bloodshed.
Meaning violence, cruelty, injustice, ruthless destruction.
Genesis says the world became saturated with it.
And that is why judgment came.
But because sin had reached catastrophic proportions.
Why This Ancient Story Feels So Modern
Genesis 6 does not feel ancient because human hearts have not fundamentally changed.
The Bible's concern is never satisfying curiosity.
The story does not end in judgment.
Genesis introduces Noah as a man who found grace.
And centuries later another invitation would come through Jesus Christ.
Noah's ark carried people through judgment.
Jesus carries believers through a far greater one.
The apostle Peter intentionally connects Noah's story to salvation through Christ.
The ark was never merely about surviving a flood.
It was a shadow of a coming Savior.
So Were the Nephilim Really Giants?
But Scripture does not provide enough information for dogmatic certainty.
Faithful Christians continue to debate the details.
But the Bible's central message remains crystal clear.
The greatest threat in Genesis 6 was never the Nephilim.
And the greatest hope was never understanding a mystery.
Many people spend their lives chasing hidden secrets in Scripture while ignoring the Savior standing in plain sight.
The Bible was never written to satisfy endless speculation.
It was written to reveal Jesus Christ.
Perhaps that is why the Nephilim appear briefly and then fade into the background.
Because even the Bible's greatest mysteries are ultimately meant to point us toward its greatest certainty.
The grace that is still available today.
Maybe the most important question was never whether the Nephilim were giants.
Maybe the most important question is whether we recognize our need for the Savior who is greater than every mystery.
Because one day every unanswered question will finally be resolved.
But only one answer determines eternity.
The greatest mystery in Genesis was never who the Nephilim were—it was why a holy God still chose to save sinners.
